items.statement: Lemma 1 (from earlier in paper): Mediation ranges that are consistent with conditions (6.2)-(6.4) cannot include any codominated actions.
items.context: Lemma 1 from earlier in the paper, invoked in the proofs of Lemma 4 and Theorem 2 to establish that mediation ranges consistent with sequential rationality must exclude codominated actions.

items.statement: Lemma 2 (from earlier in paper): There exist a correspondence B, a sequence of equilibria {σ_j} of ε_j-perturbed games with full support over G(Q) × T, and a conditional probability system δ such that δ is generated by {σ_j} as ε_j → 0 (in the sense of Theorem 1), conditions (6.2)-(6.4) are satisfied by Q and δ, and the correspondence B captures the relevant action restrictions.
items.context: Lemma 2 provides the starting point for Lemma 3's proof. The end of its proof appears at the beginning of this text: dynamics consistency (6.2) holds because trembles go to zero, and incentive constraints (6.3)-(6.4) hold because each σ_j is an equilibrium of the ε_j-perturbed game with every information state occurring with positive probability.

notation_in_scope.B: correspondence mapping type profiles to subsets of actions
notation_in_scope.σ_j: equilibrium of ε_j-perturbed game with full support over G(Q) × T

items.statement: Theorem 1 (from earlier in paper): Given a sequence of probability distributions with full support over a finite set, by choosing a subsequence if necessary, the sequence generates a conditional probability system in the limit — that is, for every event with positive probability under some distribution in the sequence, the conditional probabilities converge.
items.context: Theorem 1 is used repeatedly throughout Section 7 to extract conditional probability systems from converging sequences of full-support distributions.

items.statement: There exist B, Q, and μ such that μ is a conditional probability system on G(Q) × T, conditions (6.2)-(6.4) are satisfied by Q and μ, B is a codomination correspondence, and Q_i = {(c_i, t_i) ∈ C_i × T | c_{ik} ∉ B(t_{-k}) ∀k}, for all i.
items.proof: Let B, σ_j, and δ be as in Lemma 2 and its proof. If B is a codomination correspondence, then we are done; so suppose that it is not. Let B⁰ = B. Then there must exist some finite sequence of correspondences (B¹, ..., Bᴴ) such that Bᴴ is a codomination correspondence, Bʰ(t_{-k}) ⊆ Bʰ⁻¹(t_{-k}) for all i, k, t_{-k} ∈ T_{-k}, h ∈ {1,...,H}, and for every h and every k, there exists some probability distribution π^{hk} such that π^{hk}(Eᵏ(Bʰ⁻¹) × T_{-k}) = 1 and, for every player i and every t_{-ik} ∈ T_{-ik}: π^{hk}(f, t_{-k})(c_{ik}) > 0 implies c_{ik} ∈ Bʰ⁻¹(t_{-k})\Bʰ(t_{-k}); π^{hk}(f, t_{-k})(c_{ik}) = 0 for all c_{ik} ∈ Bʰ(t_{-k}); and the weighted incentive constraint holds for all (y'_i, r_i) ∈ M*_{i,k}. These Bʰ and π^{hk} are constructed inductively: if Bʰ⁻¹ is not a codomination correspondence, then there exists some stage ℓ and some probability distribution π such that condition (7.3) is satisfied (for B = Bʰ⁻¹ and k = ℓ) but condition (7.4) does not hold. Then let π^{hℓ} = π and Bʰ(t_{-ℓ}) = {c_{iℓ} ∈ Bʰ⁻¹(t_{-ℓ}) | π(c_{iℓ}, t_{-ℓ}) = 0}. For every stage k ≠ ℓ, let π^{hk}(f, t_{-k}) = π^{h-1,k}(f, t_{-k}) and Bʰ(t_{-k}) = Bʰ⁻¹(t_{-k}). The nonnegative integer Σ_i Σ_k Σ_{t_{-k}} |Bʰ(t_{-k})| strictly decreases with every increase in h, so the construction must terminate at a codomination correspondence. Let B = Bᴴ and let Q be derived accordingly. Define G_k(Q) and extend each π^{hk} to G(Q) × T consistently with game dynamics. By renumbering {σ_j} if necessary, assume σ_j(f,t) ≥ 1/j for all f ∈ G(Q), t ∈ T. Define δ_j(f,t) = σ_j(f,t) + Σ_{k=1}^K Σ_{h=1}^H (1/j)^{(k-1)H+h+1} · π^{hk}(f,t). The limiting conditional probabilities from {δ_j} satisfy (6.2)-(6.4) for all positive-probability events. To achieve full support, define I^k(t_{-k}), w^{<k}(t_{-k}), P^k(f), ξ_j(f,t), and then Z = KH+H+1, A_j(f,t) = Σ_{ℓ=1}^{K+1} Σ_{m=1}^{K+1} (1/j)^{Z·(ℓ-1)+(m-1)} · ξ_j^{ℓ,m}(f,t), and η_j(f,t) = A_j(f,t) / Σ_{g,s} A_j(g,s). Each η_j has full support over G(Q) × T. Let μ be the conditional probability system generated by {η_j} as j → ∞ (Theorem 1). Verification that μ satisfies (6.2)-(6.4) follows by analyzing which term in A_j has the lowest power of (1/j) for each event.

notation_in_scope.G(Q): set of feedback rules consistent with mediation range Q
notation_in_scope.μ: conditional probability system on G(Q) × T
notation_in_scope.Q_i: set of action-type pairs for player i excluding codominated actions under B
notation_in_scope.Bʰ: h-th correspondence in the inductive refinement
notation_in_scope.π^{hk}: probability distribution used at step h for stage k
notation_in_scope.E_k(B): set of outcomes where no player uses a codominated action (under B) after stage k
notation_in_scope.M*_{i,k}: set of manipulative strategies for player i at stage k

items.statement: The correspondence that always selects the empty set (i.e., B(t_{-k}) = ∅ for all t_{-k}) is a codomination correspondence.
items.proof_sketch: Vacuously satisfies the codomination conditions since there are no actions in B(t_{-k}) to check.
items.context: Stated parenthetically in the proof of Lemma 3 to justify that the inductive refinement must terminate: 'Notice that the correspondence that always selects the empty set is a codomination correspondence.'

notation_in_scope.B: correspondence mapping opponent type profiles to sets of codominated actions
notation_in_scope.t_{-k}: type profile of players other than those at stage k

items.statement: In the inductive construction of correspondences (B⁰, B¹, ..., Bᴴ) in the proof of Lemma 3, the nonnegative integer Σ_i Σ_k Σ_{t_{-k}} |Bʰ(t_{-k})| strictly decreases with every increase in h. Consequently, the construction must terminate in finitely many steps at a codomination correspondence Bᴴ.
items.proof_sketch: At each step h, Bʰ(t_{-ℓ}) is a strict subset of Bʰ⁻¹(t_{-ℓ}) for the relevant stage ℓ (removing actions with zero probability under π), while Bʰ(t_{-k}) = Bʰ⁻¹(t_{-k}) for k ≠ ℓ. Since the total count is a nonnegative integer that strictly decreases, it must reach a fixed point. The empty set correspondence is a codomination correspondence, so the process terminates at one.
items.context: Establishes finite termination of the inductive refinement of codomination correspondences in the proof of Lemma 3.

notation_in_scope.Bʰ: h-th correspondence in the inductive sequence
notation_in_scope.|Bʰ(t_{-k})|: cardinality of the set of codominated actions for type profile t_{-k} under Bʰ

items.statement: G_k(Q) = {f ∈ F | ∃g ∈ G(Q) such that f^ℓ = g^ℓ ∀ℓ < k}. That is, G_k(Q) is the set of all feedback rules that agree with some rule in G(Q) in every stage before stage k.
items.context: Introduced in the proof of Lemma 3 to define the set of feedback rules that 'look like' rules in G(Q) up to but not including stage k. Used to extend π^{hk} and in the construction of the full-support distributions.

notation_in_scope.G_k(Q): set of feedback rules consistent with Q before stage k
notation_in_scope.G(Q): set of feedback rules fully consistent with Q

items.statement: Each π^{hk} can be extended to a probability distribution over G(Q) × T by letting π^{hk}(f, t) = π^{hk}(f^k, t_{-k}) · P(t_k | f, t_{<k}), making π^{hk} consistent with the given dynamics of the game after stage k. Furthermore, since no properties of f^ℓ for ℓ < k were used in the construction of the π^{hk} values, one can assume without loss of generality that π^{hk}(f, t) = 0 if f ∉ G_k(Q), and π^{hk}(f, t) = π^{hk}(g, t) whenever f, g ∈ G_k(Q) and f^ℓ = g^ℓ for all ℓ ≥ k.
items.proof_sketch: The extension uses the game dynamics P(t_k | f, t_{<k}) after stage k. The WLOG assumption follows because the original π^{hk} values depend only on f^k and t_{-k}, not on earlier stages.
items.context: Stated in the proof of Lemma 3 after defining G_k(Q). The extension ensures π^{hk} is a proper distribution over G(Q) × T and that its marginal before stage k is uniform over G(Q).

notation_in_scope.π^{hk}: probability distribution for step h at stage k, extended to G(Q) × T
notation_in_scope.G_k(Q): feedback rules consistent with Q before stage k

items.statement: Under the WLOG assumptions, for the components of the feedback rule before stage k, π^{hk} gives the same marginal distribution as the uniform distribution on G(Q).
items.proof_sketch: Since π^{hk}(f, t) = π^{hk}(g, t) whenever f and g agree on stages ≥ k and both belong to G_k(Q), and π^{hk} vanishes outside G_k(Q), the marginal over pre-stage-k feedback components is uniform over G(Q).
items.context: Consequence of the WLOG normalization of π^{hk}, used to ensure the later perturbation construction has the right support properties.

notation_in_scope.π^{hk}: extended probability distribution for step h at stage k
notation_in_scope.G(Q): set of feedback rules consistent with Q

items.statement: For each j, define δ_j as a probability distribution over G(Q) × T by δ_j(f, t) = σ_j(f, t) + Σ_{k=1}^K Σ_{h=1}^H (1/j)^{(k-1)H+h+1} · π^{hk}(f, t), where K is the number of stages, H is the number of inductive refinement steps, σ_j are the equilibria from Lemma 2, and π^{hk} are the extended distributions from the codomination refinement.
items.context: Intermediate construction in the proof of Lemma 3. The δ_j distributions combine the equilibrium distributions σ_j with weighted contributions from the π^{hk} distributions, using decreasing powers of (1/j) to create a hierarchy. This ensures that conditional probabilities at zero-probability events are determined by the appropriate π^{hk}. The sequence {σ_j} is renumbered so that σ_j(f,t) ≥ 1/j for all f ∈ G(Q), t ∈ T.

notation_in_scope.δ_j: intermediate probability distribution combining σ_j and π^{hk}
notation_in_scope.σ_j: equilibrium of ε_j-perturbed game from Lemma 2
notation_in_scope.π^{hk}: extended distribution for refinement step h at stage k

items.statement: Given any event that has positive probability under σ_j, the conditional probabilities generated by δ_j approach those generated by σ_j as j becomes large. For events (f^{≤k}, t_{-k}) that have positive probability under δ_j but zero probability under σ_j, the conditional probabilities generated by δ_j approach (as j → ∞) those generated by the first π^{hℓ} distribution in which the event has positive probability, where 'first' means the lowest possible ℓ, and then lowest h given that ℓ.
items.proof_sketch: The σ_j term in δ_j has coefficient 1 while each π^{hk} term has coefficient (1/j)^{(k-1)H+h+1} → 0. Thus σ_j dominates for events with positive σ_j-probability. For zero-probability events under σ_j, the lowest-order π^{hk} term dominates.
items.context: Key structural property of the δ_j construction, establishing that conditional probabilities at different events are determined by the appropriate component of the hierarchical construction.

notation_in_scope.π^{hℓ}: distribution from refinement step h at stage ℓ

items.statement: The first π^{hℓ} that gives (f^{≤k}, t_{-k}) positive probability must satisfy ℓ ≤ k whenever σ_j gives zero probability to (f^{≤k}, t_{-k}). This is because when ℓ > k, π^{hℓ} gives positive probability to (f^{≤k}, t_{-k}) only if σ_j does also.
items.proof_sketch: When ℓ > k, the extension of π^{hℓ} to stages before ℓ uses the same marginal distribution as the uniform distribution on G(Q), which coincides with σ_j's support. Thus π^{hℓ} can give positive probability to a pre-stage-k event only if σ_j does.
items.context: Used in the proof of Lemma 3 to ensure that the determining π^{hℓ} for any event at or before stage k operates at a stage ℓ ≤ k, which is critical for the dynamics-consistency verification.

notation_in_scope.π^{hℓ}: distribution from refinement step h at stage ℓ
notation_in_scope.t_{-k}: opponent type profile at stage k

items.statement: In any event that has positive probability under all δ_j, the conditions (6.2)-(6.4) are satisfied by the limiting conditional probability system generated by {δ_j} as j → ∞. The dynamics-consistency condition (6.2) is satisfied because each π^{hℓ} satisfies it in every stage k ≥ ℓ. The incentive constraints (6.3)-(6.4) are satisfied because, if π^{hℓ} is the first to give positive probability to the event that player i observes (c_{ik}, t_{ik}) through the end of stage k, then ℓ ≤ k and c_{ik} ∈ Bʰ⁻¹(t_{-k})\Bʰ(t_{-k}); and π^{hℓ} was constructed so that no player could expect to gain by manipulating in any event observable with positive probability after receiving recommendation c_{ik} in state t_{-ik}.
items.proof_sketch: Dynamics consistency follows from each π^{hℓ} being consistent with game dynamics after stage ℓ. Incentive compatibility follows from the inductive construction of π^{hℓ}: condition (7.3) was required to hold, ensuring the weighted incentive constraint.
items.context: Establishes that the intermediate δ_j construction already achieves (6.2)-(6.4) for events with positive probability. However, not all histories in Q*_k necessarily have positive probability under δ_j, motivating the further perturbation to η_j.

notation_in_scope.π^{hℓ}: distribution from refinement step h at stage ℓ

items.statement: If c_{ik} is not in B(t_{-k}) (i.e., Bᴴ(t_{-k})), then there is positive probability under every δ_j that c_{ik} will be recommended at stage k to type t_{ik} of player i, after some history of past recommendations c^{≤k-1}; but not necessarily after every c^{≤k-1} such that (c^{≤k}, t_{-k}) ∈ Q*_k. The {δ_j} sequence must therefore be perturbed so that every history (c^{≤k}, t_{-k}) in Q*_k has positive probability, without losing incentive compatibility in the limit, and these perturbed distributions should have full support over G(Q) × T.
items.proof_sketch: Since c_{ik} ∉ B(t_{-k}), the equilibrium σ_j recommends c_{ik} with positive probability for some histories but the extension to all histories in Q*_k is not guaranteed.
items.context: This observation motivates the second phase of the construction in Lemma 3's proof: the need to perturb {δ_j} to achieve full support over G(Q) × T while preserving (6.2)-(6.4).

notation_in_scope.Q*_k: set of recommendation-type pairs at stage k consistent with Q
notation_in_scope.c_{ik}: recommendation to player i at stage k

items.statement: For the full-support perturbation in the proof of Lemma 3, define: (1) I^k(t_{-k}) = {f^{<k} | ∃(g, τ) such that g^k = f^k, τ_{-k} = t_{-k}, and δ_j(g, τ) > 0}, the set of pre-stage-k feedback histories with positive probability under δ_j given opponent types t_{-k}; (2) w^{<k}(t_{-k}) = Σ_{ℓ=1}^{k-1} |I^ℓ(t_{-ℓ})|, a cumulative count; (3) P^k(f) = {g ∈ F | ∀ℓ > k, g^ℓ = f^ℓ}, the set of feedback rules agreeing with f after stage k; (4) ξ_j(f, t) = δ_j(f, t) / |I^{<k}(t_{-k})| if f^{<k} ∈ I^{<k}(t_{-k}), and 0 otherwise.
items.context: These auxiliary quantities are introduced to reweight the δ_j distributions for the full-support construction. I^k identifies which pre-stage-k histories have positive probability; ξ_j reweights δ_j to equalize pre-stage-k marginals across histories.

notation_in_scope.I^k(t_{-k}): consistent feedback histories before stage k
notation_in_scope.P^k(f): feedback rules agreeing with f after stage k

items.statement: For the full-support perturbation in the proof of Lemma 3, define: Z = KH + H + 1 (chosen to exceed the highest power of (1/j) in δ_j); A_j(f, t) = Σ_{ℓ=1}^{K+1} Σ_{m=1}^{K+1} (1/j)^{Z·(ℓ-1)+(m-1)} · ξ_j^{ℓ,m}(f, t); and η_j(f, t) = A_j(f, t) / Σ_{g ∈ G(Q)} Σ_{s ∈ T} A_j(g, s). For each j, η_j is a probability distribution with full support over G(Q) × T.
items.context: The perturbation A_j combines multiple reweighted distributions at different powers of (1/j), ensuring full support and allowing the limiting conditional probability system to satisfy the required conditions. The normalization η_j is the final sequence used to generate μ via Theorem 1.

notation_in_scope.Z: KH + H + 1, exceeds highest power of (1/j) in δ_j
notation_in_scope.η_j: normalized probability distribution with full support over G(Q) × T
notation_in_scope.H: number of steps in the inductive refinement
notation_in_scope.ξ_j^{ℓ,m}: reweighted distribution component for stages ℓ and m

items.statement: For each j, η_j is a probability distribution with full support over G(Q) × T.
items.proof_sketch: Full support follows from the construction: by letting P(t_k | f, t_{<k}) = (uniform) when m = K+1 in the definition of ξ_j^{ℓ,m}, every point in G(Q) × T receives positive probability under A_j, and hence under η_j.
items.context: The full support property of η_j is essential: it ensures that the limiting conditional probability system μ (from Theorem 1) is well-defined for all events in G(Q) × T, and that (6.2) can be verified for all conditioning events.

notation_in_scope.G(Q): set of feedback rules consistent with Q

items.statement: The distribution ξ_j^k can be interpreted as the joint distribution of a manifest mediator's feedback rule and the game outcome under the following procedure: two mediators exist, one manifest and one subliminal. The players are coordinated by the subliminal mediator throughout the game according to the δ_j distribution. In stage k and thereafter, the manifest mediator uses the same feedback rule as the subliminal mediator. Before stage k, the manifest mediator selects his feedback function for stage ℓ uniformly at random from I^k(t_{-ℓ}), given the current information state t_{-ℓ}.
items.context: This interpretation provides the game-theoretic intuition for the technical construction of ξ_j. It clarifies why the construction preserves incentive compatibility: the subliminal mediator maintains equilibrium properties while the manifest mediator's deviations before stage k are invisible to conditional beliefs at and after stage k.

notation_in_scope.I^k(t_{-ℓ}): manifest mediator's available feedback functions before stage k

items.statement: For any event X ⊂ G(Q) × T, the conditional probabilities μ(·|X) generated by the sequence {η_j} as j → ∞ are completely determined by the term in the definition of A_j that has the lowest power of (1/j) among all terms that are positive for at least one point in X.
items.proof_sketch: Since Z exceeds the highest power of (1/j) in δ_j, the terms in A_j with the lowest exponent dominate the conditional probability calculation as j → ∞. All higher-order terms vanish relative to the dominant term.
items.context: This is the key structural insight in the proof of Lemma 3: the layered polynomial construction of A_j ensures that conditional beliefs at zero-probability events are determined by the appropriate layer of perturbation.

notation_in_scope.μ: conditional probability system generated as j → ∞

items.statement: Any event (f^{≤k}, t_{-k}) that has positive probability under ξ_j^ℓ for some ℓ > k must also have positive probability under ξ_j^k, because of the definition of I^k(t_{-k}).
items.proof_sketch: When ℓ > k, the distribution ξ_j^ℓ gives positive probability to (f^{≤k}, t_{-k}) only if δ_j does so as well, since I^k(t_{-k}) is defined from the support of δ_j. And if δ_j gives positive probability to (f^{≤k}, t_{-k}), then ξ_j^k does as well by construction.
items.context: Used in verifying the dynamics-consistency condition (6.2) for the conditional probability system μ. This ensures that the determining term for any pre-stage-k event comes from a stage ℓ ≤ k.

notation_in_scope.I^k(t_{-k}): set of pre-stage-k feedback histories with positive probability under δ_j

items.statement: The conditional probability system μ constructed via {η_j} satisfies the dynamics-consistency condition (6.2). Specifically: if f^{<ℓ} ∈ I^{<ℓ}(t_{-ℓ}) for every ℓ ≤ k (for all j sufficiently large), then the conditional probabilities μ(·|f^{≤k}, t_{-k}) are determined by the {δ_j} sequence for some ℓ ≤ k, and are consistent with the dynamics of the game after that stage (since the manifest and subliminal mediators coincide from stage ℓ onward). If f^{<ℓ} ∉ I^{<ℓ}(t_{-ℓ}) for some ℓ ≤ k, let m be the lowest such ℓ with the appropriate positive probability condition; then m ≤ k and the conditional probabilities μ(·|f^{≤k}, t_{-k}) are completely determined by the term for m in the second summation of A_j. In both cases (6.2) is satisfied.
items.proof_sketch: The dynamics-consistency follows because each ξ_j^ℓ is consistent with the game dynamics after stage ℓ (when the manifest and subliminal mediators coincide). The claim that the determining ℓ satisfies ℓ ≤ k follows from Claim_L3_j.
items.context: First verification step for the conditional probability system μ in the proof of Lemma 3.

notation_in_scope.μ: conditional probability system on G(Q) × T
notation_in_scope.I^{<ℓ}(t_{-ℓ}): consistent feedback histories before stage ℓ

items.statement: The conditional probability system μ constructed via {η_j} satisfies the incentive constraints (6.3) and (6.4). For any player i and any (c^{≤k}, t_{-k}) in Q*_k, let ℓ be the highest stage number such that the recommendation c_{iℓ} would have zero probability under the δ_j distributions for all j sufficiently large. Then ℓ ≤ k, and player i's conditional beliefs μ(·|c^{≤k}, t_{-k}) are completely determined by the {δ_j} sequence. Player i believes that although the manifest mediator diverged from the subliminal mediator before stage ℓ, the conditional probabilities generated by {δ_j} as j → ∞ accurately characterize the current state from stage ℓ onward. Since the relevant incentive constraints were satisfied by the beliefs generated by {δ_j}, μ satisfies (6.3) and (6.4).
items.proof_sketch: The determining π^{hℓ} satisfies ℓ ≤ k and c_{ik} ∈ Bʰ⁻¹(t_{-k})\Bʰ(t_{-k}), and was constructed so that no player could expect to gain by manipulating after receiving recommendation c_{ik} in state t_{-ik}.
items.context: Second verification step for the conditional probability system μ in the proof of Lemma 3, completing the proof.

notation_in_scope.c_{ik}: recommendation to player i at stage k
notation_in_scope.t_{-k}: opponent type profile at stage k
notation_in_scope.Q*_k: set of recommendation-type pairs at stage k consistent with Q

items.statement: Let B and Q be as in Lemma 3, and let D and Q̃ be as defined in Section 7 (where D is the maximal codomination correspondence and Q̃ is the maximal mediation range). Then B = D and Q = Q̃.
items.proof: By Lemma 1, mediation ranges that are consistent with (6.2)-(6.4) cannot include any codominated actions. By Lemma 3, Q is consistent with (6.2)-(6.4) and, in every state, allows all the actions that are not in the codomination correspondence B. Thus, B is equal to D, the maximal codomination correspondence, and Q is equal to Q̃. Q.E.D.

items.statement: G(Q̃) = E⁰(D), where Q̃ is the mediation range derived from the maximal codomination correspondence D, G(Q̃) is the set of feedback rules consistent with Q̃, and E⁰(D) is the set of outcomes where no player ever uses a codominated action under D.
items.proof_sketch: Follows from the definitions: G(Q̃) restricts feedback rules to avoid codominated actions in every stage, which is precisely E⁰(D).
items.context: Parenthetical identification stated in the proof of Theorem 2: 'Recall G(Q̃) = E⁰(D).' This equates two key notations used in the characterization theorem.

notation_in_scope.G(Q̃): set of feedback rules consistent with Q̃
notation_in_scope.E⁰(D): set of outcomes where no player uses codominated actions in any stage

items.statement: A communication equilibrium μ is a sequential communication equilibrium if and only if μ(E⁰(D)) = 1, where D is the maximal codomination correspondence and E⁰(D) is the set of outcomes where no player ever uses a codominated action under D.
items.proof: If μ is a sequential communication equilibrium, then there is some mediation range Q on which (6.2)-(6.4) can be satisfied and such that μ(G(Q)) = 1. But by Lemma 1, Q ⊆ Q̃, because Q must avoid all codominated actions, and so μ(G(Q̃)) = 1. (Recall G(Q̃) = E⁰(D).) Conversely, suppose that μ is a communication equilibrium and μ(G(Q̃)) = 1. Let η_j be as in the proof of Lemma 3. Then define a sequence of probability distributions p_j with full support over G(Q̃) × T: p_j(f, t) = (1 - 1/j) · μ(f) · P(t|f) + (1/j) · η_j(f, t). Let μ̃ be the conditional probability system generated by p_j as j → ∞. For any event X, the conditional probabilities μ̃(·|X) are the same as under μ · P if X has positive probability under μ · P; otherwise the conditional probabilities are the same as those generated by the η_j as j → ∞. But μ · P is consistent with the given dynamics of the game, and satisfies the incentive constraints in all events that have positive probability, since μ is a communication equilibrium. As shown in the proof of Lemma 3, the η_j generate conditional probabilities that satisfy (6.2)-(6.4) with the mediation range Q̃. Thus, (6.2)-(6.4) are satisfied by μ̃ and Q̃, and (6.1) follows immediately from the definition of p_j. Q.E.D.
items.context: The proof header states 'PROOF OF THEOREM 2 AND COROLLARY 1', indicating that Corollary 1 (stated earlier in the paper) is also established by this argument.

notation_in_scope.E⁰(D): set of outcomes where no player uses codominated actions in any stage
notation_in_scope.G(Q̃): set of feedback rules consistent with Q̃, equal to E⁰(D)
notation_in_scope.P(t|f): probability of types given feedback rule (game dynamics)
notation_in_scope.μ̃: conditional probability system generated by p_j as j → ∞

items.statement: Corollary 1 (statement from earlier in paper). Proved jointly with Theorem 2.
items.proof_sketch: Proved alongside Theorem 2; the same argument establishes both results.
items.context: Referenced in the proof header 'PROOF OF THEOREM 2 AND COROLLARY 1'. The full statement of Corollary 1 appears in an earlier part of the paper not included in this excerpt.

items.statement: In the proof of Theorem 2 (converse direction), the conditional probability system μ̃ generated by p_j(f, t) = (1 - 1/j) · μ(f) · P(t|f) + (1/j) · η_j(f, t) as j → ∞ has the property that: for any event X with positive probability under μ · P, the conditional probabilities μ̃(·|X) equal those under μ · P; for any event X with zero probability under μ · P, the conditional probabilities μ̃(·|X) equal those generated by {η_j} as j → ∞.
items.proof_sketch: Since (1 - 1/j) dominates (1/j) as j → ∞, events with positive probability under μ · P have their conditional probabilities determined by the μ · P component. Events with zero probability under μ · P but positive probability under η_j have their conditional probabilities determined by the η_j component.
items.context: Key observation in the converse direction of Theorem 2's proof. The constructed conditional probability system μ̃ inherits incentive compatibility from μ on the equilibrium path and from Lemma 3's construction off the path.

notation_in_scope.μ̃: limiting conditional probability system from p_j
notation_in_scope.μ · P: product of equilibrium distribution and game dynamics

items.statement: If μ(E⁰(D)) = 1 and μ satisfies condition (4.1) for every player i and every manipulative strategy (y_i, r_i) in L_i, then μ is a sequential communication equilibrium.
items.proof: Suppose, contrary to the theorem, that μ(E⁰(D)) = 1 and μ satisfies (4.1) for every (y_i, r_i) in L_i, but μ is not a communication equilibrium. Then there exists some player i who could expect (ex ante) to gain by using some manipulative strategy that uses codominated actions with positive probability. Among the (finitely many) manipulative strategies that are optimal for player i against μ, choose (y_i, r_i) so that, for the lowest possible number k, y_i would never select a codominated action after stage k. Let ν be the mechanism that effectively results when player i manipulates μ by (y_i, r_i), so that ν(f) = μ({g | g ∘ (y_i, r_i) = f}). Let π be the probability distribution over F × T_{-k} induced by ν, so that π(f, t_{-k}) = Σ ν(f) · P(t|f). Notice that π(E^k(D) × T_{-k}) = 1, since no player is being told to use codominated actions after stage k. Also, π(Ē_k(D)) > 0, because player i must be using codominated actions with positive probability in stage k. (If player i were using codominated actions in stage k with zero probability only, then we could find another manipulative strategy that is also optimal for i against μ and that never uses codominated actions after stage k − 1, contradicting the minimality of k.) Thus, by definition of codomination, there must be some player who can expect to gain by planning to manipulate against π after getting a recommendation to use a codominated action at stage k. But that player must be player i, because no other player ever gets a codominated recommendation under π. But if player i could expect to gain by planning to manipulate against π, then (y_i, r_i) could not have been an optimal manipulation against μ. This contradiction proves the theorem. Q.E.D.

notation_in_scope.E⁰(D): set of outcomes where no player uses codominated actions
notation_in_scope.L_i: set of manipulative strategies for player i (defined in condition 4.1)
notation_in_scope.(y_i, r_i): manipulative strategy: y_i selects actions, r_i reports types
notation_in_scope.E^k(D): outcomes where no codominated actions are used after stage k
notation_in_scope.Ē_k(D): event that some codominated action is used at stage k

items.statement: If (y_i, r_i) is a manipulative strategy for player i such that y_i never selects a codominated action after stage k, and ν is the mechanism that effectively results when player i manipulates μ by (y_i, r_i), and π is the distribution induced by ν over F × T_{-k}, then π(E^k(D) × T_{-k}) = 1.
items.proof_sketch: Since no player is being told to use codominated actions after stage k under the induced mechanism ν, the support of π is contained in E^k(D) × T_{-k}.
items.context: Used in the proof of Theorem 3. The manipulative strategy (y_i, r_i) is chosen with the property that y_i never selects a codominated action after stage k, which ensures the induced distribution concentrates on outcomes without codominated actions from stage k onward.

notation_in_scope.y_i: action selection rule in manipulative strategy
notation_in_scope.ν: effective mechanism under manipulation by (y_i, r_i)
notation_in_scope.E^k(D): event that no codominated actions used from stage k onward
notation_in_scope.k: lowest stage after which y_i avoids codominated actions

items.statement: Under the same setup, if k is the minimal stage such that (y_i, r_i) never selects a codominated action after stage k, then π(Ē_k(D)) > 0, i.e., player i uses codominated actions with positive probability at stage k.
items.proof_sketch: If player i were using codominated actions in stage k with zero probability, then we could find another manipulative strategy that is also optimal for i against μ and that never uses codominated actions after stage k − 1, contradicting the minimality of k.
items.context: Key step in the proof by contradiction of Theorem 3. The minimality of k forces player i to actually use codominated actions at stage k, which triggers the codomination condition.

notation_in_scope.Ē_k(D): event that some codominated action is used at stage k
notation_in_scope.k: minimal stage index for codominated action avoidance
notation_in_scope.(y_i, r_i): optimal manipulative strategy for player i

items.statement: Under the induced distribution π from the manipulative strategy (y_i, r_i), the only player who ever receives a recommendation to use a codominated action is player i. No other player j ≠ i ever gets a codominated recommendation under π.
items.proof_sketch: The original mechanism μ satisfies μ(E⁰(D)) = 1, meaning μ never recommends codominated actions to any player. The manipulation (y_i, r_i) only alters player i's behavior — other players' recommendations come directly from μ and hence are never codominated.
items.context: Crucial observation for the final contradiction in Theorem 3's proof: since the codomination condition implies some player can gain by deviating after receiving a codominated recommendation at stage k, and only player i receives such recommendations, the deviating player must be player i — but this contradicts the optimality of (y_i, r_i).

notation_in_scope.π: induced distribution under player i's manipulation
notation_in_scope.E⁰(D): set of outcomes avoiding all codominated actions

items.statement: If π(Ē_k(D)) > 0 (codominated actions are used at stage k with positive probability) and π(E^k(D) × T_{-k}) = 1 (no codominated actions after stage k), then by the definition of codomination, there exists some player who can expect to gain by planning to manipulate against π (equivalently, against ν) after receiving a recommendation to use a codominated action at stage k.
items.proof_sketch: This follows directly from the definition of codomination correspondence: if a probability distribution gives positive probability to codominated actions at some stage but avoids them thereafter, the codomination conditions guarantee the existence of a profitable deviation for some player at that stage.
items.context: The penultimate step of the contradiction argument in Theorem 3's proof. Combined with Claim_T3_c (only player i gets codominated recommendations), this implies player i can profitably deviate from (y_i, r_i), contradicting its optimality.

notation_in_scope.Ē_k(D): event of codominated actions at stage k
notation_in_scope.E^k(D): event of no codominated actions from stage k onward
